lead: An engine must fire the spark and open each injector at a precise crank angle, not just at a precise average rate. The crankshaft position sensor (CKP) and the camshaft position sensor (CMP) report piston position and engine speed to the engine control unit (ECU). The ECU uses these pulses to synchronise ignition and fuel delivery, to detect misfire, and to run sequential injection. Every modern petrol engine uses at least a CKP. Some syllabi call the CKP the engine crankshaft angular position sensor, the engine angular speed sensor or the timing sensor.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for threshold and filter circuits, and basic angular motion: angle in degrees, speed in rpm and frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: The CKP faces a toothed wheel on the crankshaft pulley or the flywheel. Each tooth that passes the sensor produces one electrical pulse. The ECU reads angular position from the identity of the tooth and angular speed from the time between pulses. The same signal gives both quantities, so one sensor serves ignition timing, injector timing, idle control, the rev limiter and the tachometer.

The CMP reads a single tooth, window or magnetic target on the camshaft. In a four-stroke engine the camshaft turns at half crankshaft speed, so one cam pulse occurs per two crank revolutions. That pulse identifies cylinder 1 on its compression stroke. Sequential fuel injection and individual coil-on-plug ignition need this phase information; without it the ECU may fall back to wasted spark (spark on both strokes) and batch injection (injectors fired in groups).

Angular position is an angle, usually measured in degrees before top dead centre (BTDC). Angular speed is a rate, usually in revolutions per minute (rpm). Do not mix them. A CKP can report position to within one tooth pitch and speed to within a fraction of a percent after filtering.

blocks.where: n is revolutions per second; rpm is revolutions per minute; z is the number of tooth pitches per revolution (60 for a 60-2 wheel, 36 for a 36-1 wheel); T is the time between successive normal tooth edges in seconds; Δθ is the crank angle per tooth pitch in degrees. For a 60-2 wheel Δθ = 6°.

blocks.text: A plain toothed wheel gives speed but not absolute position: the ECU cannot tell tooth 1 from tooth 20 after switch-on. Manufacturers cut one or more teeth out of the wheel to create a reference gap. Common wheels are 60-2 (58 teeth present, 2 missing), 36-1 (35 present, 1 missing) and 12+1. In a 12+1 wheel all teeth are present, and the reference is the single short interval produced by the extra tooth, so the ECU detects an unusually short period instead of an unusually long one. The reference feature appears once per revolution.

items: Condition the sensor signal into clean edges (see 3.1).
Measure the period T between consecutive edges with a timer.
Compare each period with the previous one. A gap is longer than a normal tooth period by a known ratio: for 60-2 the gap is 3T.
When the gap is detected, reset the tooth counter and assign the stored angle of the first tooth after the gap.
Compute speed from T and update the ignition and injection schedules.

blocks.text: The missing-tooth gap for a 60-2 wheel is three tooth periods, not two. The last present tooth is followed by two empty slots and then the next present tooth, so the time from the last edge to the next edge is 3T. For a 36-1 wheel the gap is 2T. The ECU calibration stores the exact crank angle of the first tooth after the gap; that angle differs between engines.

Speed comes from the period, not from counting pulses in a fixed window. A period measurement updates once per tooth and reacts quickly during acceleration. The ECU filters very short periods to reject noise and uses a timeout to detect a stopped engine.

A variable-reluctance (VR) sensor, also called an inductive sensor, has a permanent magnet and a coil. A tooth passing the pole piece changes the magnetic flux and induces an alternating voltage. The amplitude rises with engine speed and falls with a larger air gap (the clearance between sensor tip and tooth). At cranking speed the signal may be only a few hundred millivolts, so the conditioning circuit uses a zero-crossing detector with hysteresis (two threshold levels). A VR sensor has two wires and needs no supply.

A Hall sensor has a Hall element, a magnet and a rotating vane or toothed target. It switches its output between low and high, giving a digital square wave. The amplitude is set by the supply and load, not by speed, so the ECU sees a usable signal down to zero speed. Hall CKP sensors are common on engines that must start reliably in cold weather. They have three wires: supply, ground and signal.

An optical sensor uses a light-emitting diode (LED) and a phototransistor across a slotted disc. It gives clean digital pulses but is sensitive to dirt and oil, so it is more common in test rigs and some distributor-based systems. A magnetoresistive (MR) sensor uses a thin film whose resistance changes with magnetic field direction. It gives a digital output with a large air gap and good low-speed performance, and appears in some crank and cam sensors.

Signal shape matters to the ECU. A VR output rises and falls as the tooth approaches and leaves the pole piece. Its voltage is proportional to the rate of change of flux, so it crosses zero when the tooth is centred on the pole piece and the flux is maximum. The ECU detects that zero crossing as the timing reference. The time between successive zero crossings is still one tooth pitch period T, so the speed formulas do not change. Hall, optical and MR outputs are already logic levels; their reference is the chosen signal edge. The stored calibration offset therefore differs between sensor types, and a VR sensor and a Hall sensor on the same wheel need different offsets.

figure.caption: At 3000 rpm a 60-2 wheel gives a normal tooth edge every 333 µs. The gap lasts 1.0 ms, and the ECU resets its tooth counter when the next tooth arrives.

spec.aria: Timeline at 3000 rpm of crank tooth pulses every 333 µs, with a 1.0 ms three-period missing-tooth gap and an ECU sync pulse after it.

examples.question: A 60-2 crank wheel turns at 3000 rpm. Find the time between successive normal tooth edges and the duration of the missing-tooth gap measured from the last present tooth to the first present tooth after the gap.
steps: Time for one revolution: 1 ÷ 50 = 0.020 s = 20 ms.
A 60-2 wheel has 60 tooth pitches per revolution. Normal tooth period T = 20 ms ÷ 60 = 0.333333 ms ≈ 0.333 ms.
The gap spans three pitch periods: the last present tooth, two empty slots, then the next present tooth. Gap = 3 × 0.333333 ms = 1.000 ms.
examples.answer: The normal tooth period is 0.333 ms and the missing-tooth gap is 1.0 ms.
examples.check:
rpm = 3000
z = 60
rev_per_s = rpm / 60
T_rev_s = 1 / rev_per_s
T_tooth_ms = T_rev_s / z * 1000
gap_ms = 3 * T_tooth_ms
print(round(rev_per_s, 1))
print(round(T_rev_s * 1000, 1))
print(round(T_tooth_ms, 3))
print(round(gap_ms, 3))

traps: For a 60-2 wheel the missing-tooth gap is 3T, not 2T. Two teeth are missing, but the interval from the last present tooth to the next present tooth covers three pitch periods.
Use the pitch count z (60 for 60-2, 36 for 36-1) in speed = 1/(zT). Do not use the number of present teeth (58 or 35) when you measure T between normal teeth.
VR amplitude changes with speed; a clean signal at 3000 rpm does not prove the sensor will work at 150 rpm cranking. Hall output amplitude does not depend on speed.
Angular position is an angle in degrees; angular speed is a rate in rpm. A timing sensor gives phase information, not necessarily a second independent speed signal.
Do not assume the first tooth after the gap is at TDC. Its offset is calibration data and varies between engines.

quiz.q: Name the two sensors that give crank position and cylinder phase. State the signal each provides.
quiz.a: CKP gives crank angle and engine speed; CMP gives cam phase and identifies cylinder 1 on compression.

quiz.q: Why does a 60-2 wheel need a missing-tooth gap?
quiz.a: The gap is an absolute reference once per revolution. Without it the ECU cannot tell which tooth is which after switch-on, so it cannot synchronise ignition and injection to the crank angle.

quiz.q: A 36-1 wheel turns at 1200 rpm. Find the normal tooth period and the gap duration.
quiz.a: 1200 rpm ÷ 60 = 20 rev/s. One revolution = 1/20 = 50 ms. Normal period T = 50 ms ÷ 36 = 1.389 ms. Gap = 2T = 2.778 ms.

quiz.q: A 60-2 wheel gives a normal tooth period of 500 µs. Find the engine speed in rpm.
A VR CKP gives no usable signal during cranking but works above 500 rpm. Give two likely causes and one design change.
quiz.a: Causes: cranking speed too low for the VR amplitude to reach the threshold; air gap too large or sensor tip fouled with metal debris; open or shorted winding, or a corroded connector adding series resistance. Design change: fit a Hall CKP, set the air gap to specification, or improve the threshold and gain of the conditioning circuit.

quiz.q: The CKP signal is good but the CMP fails. What happens to injection and ignition?
quiz.a: The ECU loses cylinder phase. It may run batch injection and wasted spark, so the engine may start but with less precise fuelling and timing; some systems refuse to start or set a fault code.

quiz.q: Why does the CMP turn at half crankshaft speed?
quiz.a: In a four-stroke engine the camshaft completes one turn for every two turns of the crankshaft, because the complete cycle needs four piston strokes.

quiz.q: What is edge detection in a crank sensor interface?
quiz.a: It converts a signal transition into a logic event at a chosen threshold, so the ECU can time the arrival of each tooth.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines increasingly combine crank and cam signals in one ECU model with plausibility checks, and some use ion-current or cylinder-pressure sensing. Magnetoresistive and Hall sensors with integrated signal conditioning are replacing plain VR sensors in start-stop engines. Research looks at sensorless crank angle from starter current ripple and at high-resolution crank encoders for cylinder deactivation. Search for 'crankshaft position sensor missing tooth sync', 'variable reluctance sensor threshold detection' and 'Hall effect crank sensor start-stop'.
